title: Śarīrārthagāthā
text:
**Śag_1.1**
Let one do no evil—nothing whatever—by mind, by speech, or by body anywhere in the world; void of desires, mindful, and clearly comprehending, let one not pursue suffering that is bound up with harm.
**Śag_2.1**
Beings, perceiving only {{ākhyeya:the expressible|that which can be designated or named}}, rest upon this expressible; failing to fully comprehend the expressible, they come under the yoke of death.
**Śag_2.2**
But one who has fully comprehended the expressible does not conceive of any "namer"; for him there exists nothing whereby others might speak of him.
**Śag_2.3**
Whoever conceives himself "equal," "superior," or "inferior" would, on that account, contend; but one who does not waver amid this triad of measurings—for him there is neither equality nor superiority.
**Śag_2.4**
Having cut off craving here amid {{nāmarūpa:name-and-form|the psycho-physical complex}} and abandoned conceit, he comes to no attachment; that one—his smoke of passion stilled, untroubled, free of longing—they did not behold, neither in the world of gods nor of men, neither here nor without.
**Śag_3.1**
Overpowered by sensual passion, my mind is wholly aflame; pray, Gautama, out of compassion, tell me of peace.
**Śag_3.2**
It is through the distortion of perceptions that your mind is aflame; therefore let the attractive sign that is conjoined with passion be shunned.
**Śag_3.3**
Cultivate ever the {{aśubhā(-bhāvanā):unattractive|the foulness meditation}}, one-pointed and well composed; swiftly quench the fire of passion, lest you be burned again and again.
**Śag_3.4**
See the conditioned {{saṃskāra:formations|conditioned, volitional constructs}} as wretched, as suffering, and likewise as not-self; setting up mindfulness directed to the body, abound in disgust [for them].
**Śag_3.5**
And let the {{animitta:signless|the objectless concentration that is also a gateway to liberation}} be cultivated, the destroyer of the latent tendency to conceit; then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you will make an end of suffering.
**Śag_4.1**
[The maiden's question-verse:] Dwelling in what manner does a monk, having crossed the five floods, cross here the sixth as well? Meditating in what manner does he become one who has crossed the vast craving for sensual pleasures, no longer in the grip of its harness?
**Śag_4.2**
With body tranquil and mind well liberated, constructing nothing, mindful and unshakeable—having understood the Dharma, meditating without [discursive] thought—he is freed from the faults of anger, longing, and torpor.
**Śag_4.3**
Dwelling in this manner, a monk, having crossed the five floods, crosses here the sixth as well; meditating in this manner he becomes one who has crossed the vast craving for sensual pleasures, no longer in the grip of its harness.
**Śag_5.1**
This world is ever frightened, this people ever agitated, whether by sufferings not yet arisen or by those already arisen; if there is anything at all that is unafraid, tell me, since I ask.
**Śag_5.2**
Not apart from the austerity of knowledge, not apart from restraint of the senses, not apart from the total relinquishment of all—nowhere else do I see liberation, O deity.
**Śag_5.3**
After so long, ah, I behold a {{brāhmaṇa:true brāhmaṇa|in the Buddhist sense, the saint or arhat}} fully quenched, gone beyond all enmity and fear, who has crossed the clinging that is in the world.
**Śag_6.1**
By whom is the populace extolled and led on, and the {{nairyāṇika:deliverance-leading|conducing to release}} path set forth? Established where, and training in what, does this mortal not dread the world beyond?

title: Śarīrārthagāthā
text:
**Śag_6.2**
He who is virtuous, wise, of cultivated self, composed, mindful, and upright—all his fevers of grief are abandoned, who is rightly mindful and whose mind is liberated.
**Śag_6.3**
By him is the populace extolled and led on, and the deliverance-leading path set forth; established herein, and training herein, this mortal does not dread the world beyond.
**Śag_7.1**
How does one become renowned? How does one become wealthy? How does one win repute? How does one gain friends?
**Śag_7.2**
Through virtue one becomes renowned; through giving one becomes wealthy; by truth one wins repute; by being liberal one gains friends.
**Śag_8.1**
Whence do the streams turn back? Where does the track not run? Where, in the world, does pleasure-and-pain cease without remainder?
**Śag_8.2**
Eye, ear, and nose, tongue, body, and likewise mind—[there the streams turn back;] where {{nāmarūpa:name and form|the psycho-physical complex}} both cease without remainder.
**Śag_8.3**
Thence the streams turn back; there the track does not run; there, in the world, pleasure-and-pain ceases without remainder.
**Śag_9.1**
By what does one cross the {{ogha:flood|the flood of saṃsāric defilements}}, and by what does one get across the ocean? By what does one cast off suffering? By what is one purified?
**Śag_9.2**
By faith one crosses the flood, and by diligence the ocean; by energy one casts off suffering; by wisdom one is purified.
**Śag_10.1**
Who crosses this flood, day and night untiring? Who, in the supportless, baseless deep, does not sink?
**Śag_10.2**
He who is wholly perfect in virtue, wise, well composed, inwardly reflective, and mindful—he crosses this [flood] so hard to cross.
**Śag_10.3**
Detached from the perceptions of sensual desire, gone beyond the fetter of form—he, in the supportless, baseless deep, does not sink.
**Śag_11.1**
Passion and hatred, O Blessed One—what is their source? Aversion and delight, and this horripilation—whence are they? And from what do mental musings spring up, [which] cling [to the mind] as boys cling to a nurse?
**Śag_11.2**
Born of affection, self-arisen, like the trunk-shoots of a banyan tree, severally fastened upon sensual objects, like the māluvā creeper in the forest.
**Śag_11.3**
Passion and hatred have this for their source; aversion and delight and this horripilation are from this; and from this spring up the mental musings, [which] cling [to the mind] as boys cling to a nurse.
**Śag_11.4**
Those who fully know them, [knowing] from what they are sourced—those people, O Yakṣa, dispel them; they cross over the ocean-flood here, the never-before-crossed, unto no-more-becoming.
**Śag_12.1**
This is the task to be done by the {{brāhmaṇa:true brāhmaṇa|the saint or arhat}}, who is tireless: abandoning, for the sake of the utter abandoning of sensual desires; for such a one yearns not for [renewed] becoming.
**Śag_12.2**
[Only so long as] there is a task for the brāhmaṇa [is it to be done]; the brāhmaṇa whose aim is accomplished is reckoned [as having finished his work].
**Śag_12.3**
As long as he finds no foothold and no shore, just so long he strives [to swim] with all his limbs; but having gained the shore here, he stands fast on dry ground and strives no more—he is called "gone to the far shore."
**Śag_12.4**
This, O Dāmali, is a simile for the brāhmaṇa: one whose cankers are destroyed, prudent, an attainer of meditative absorption—all his fevers of grief are abandoned, who is rightly mindful and whose mind is liberated.

title: Śarīrārthagāthā
text:
**Śag_13**
[A chant:] "Monk, monk, did you cross the {{ogha:flood|the flood of saṃsāric defilements}}?"—"Yes, deity."—"Did you cross the flood without support and without footing?"—"Yes, deity."—"In what way, monk, did you cross the flood without support and without footing?"—"In just the measure, deity, that I strove, in that measure I sank down; in just the measure that I sank down, in that measure I stood still; in just the measure that I stood still, in that measure I was swept away; [but] in just the measure, deity, that I did not strive, in that measure I did not sink down." Thus is the bright side [of the matter] to be understood in detail.
**Śag_14.1**
[The maiden's question-verse:] Alone, withdrawn into the forest, you meditate—are you bereft of wealth, or else longing for it? Or have you done some wrong against the village? Why do you make friendship with no one? Friendship with anyone at all is not found in you.
**Śag_14.2**
Through not grasping at gain there is, here, peace of heart; having conquered here the army that wears the guise of the dear and pleasant, I, meditating alone, have come to know happiness—therefore I make friendship with no one; friendship with anyone at all is not found in me.
**Śag_15**
Impermanent, alas, are the {{saṃskāra:conditioned formations|conditioned, volitional constructs}}, of the nature of arising and passing away; having arisen, they cease—their stilling is bliss.
**Śag_16**
Heedfulness is the path to the deathless; heedlessness is the path of death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if forever dead.
**Śag_17**
For the embodied one churned by [discursive] thoughts, of keen passion, contemplating the attractive, craving grows ever the more; it draws tight his bondage.
**Śag_18**
The man established in the Dharma, perfect in virtue, conscientious, truthful, who does what benefits himself—him the people hold dear.
**Śag_19**
Having here observed an evil deed done by others, one should consider [it well, and] not do the like oneself; for the evildoer is bound by his deed.
**Śag_20**
The noble ones declare the well-spoken to be supreme: let one speak the pleasant, not the unpleasant—that is the second; let one speak the truth, not falsehood—that is the third; let one speak the Dharma, not non-Dharma—that is the fourth.
**Śag_21**
Faith, then conscience, virtue, and also giving—these dharmas are praised by the good. This indeed they call the heaven-going path; by this one goes to the world of the gods.
**Śag_22**
By hearing one comes to understand the Dharma; by hearing one turns away from evil; by hearing one casts off the harmful; by hearing one attains {{nirvṛti / nirvāṇa:quenching|final extinction, peace}}.
**Śag_23**
Like space, he is not stained; like Indra's pillar, he does not tremble; like a clear lake into which mud has fallen [yet stays clear], the wise man takes no delight in saṃsāra.
**Śag_24.1**
Those who measure me by [outward] form and follow me by [mere] sound, fallen under the sway of desire and passion—those people do not know me.
**Śag_24.2**
One who understands the inward but does not see the outward, who beholds [only] the inward fruit—he indeed is led by mere sound.
**Śag_24.3**
One who does not know the inward but discerns the outward, who beholds [only] the outward fruit—he too is led by mere sound.
**Śag_24.4**
One who neither knows the inward nor sees the outward, a fool enveloped on every side—he too is led by mere sound.
**Śag_24.5**
One who understands the inward and also discerns the outward—the steadfast one, wise in the way of escape—he is not led by mere sound.

title: Śarīrārthagāthā
text:
**Śag_25**
When the sixth ruler, the king [the mind], is impassioned, one becomes dust-laden; in the dustless one becomes dustless. The impassioned one is called a fool.
**Śag_26**
A city whose ramparts are of bone, plastered over with sinew and flesh, wherein lust and hatred, conceit and hypocrisy lie lurking.
**Śag_27**
As a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell, so let the monk draw in the musings of the mind; independent, harming no others, fully quenched, let him disparage no one.
**Śag_28**
Relinquishing the formation of becoming, [the cause of] origination both equal and unequal, the sage, inwardly delighted and composed, broke [its shell] as a chick breaks the shell at its hatching from the egg.
**Śag_29**
There is no mire like lust, no seizing-demon like hatred, no net like delusion, no river like craving.
**Śag_30**
In the sky there is, truly, no track; there is no recluse outside [the teaching]. Fools delight in {{prapañca:conceptual proliferation|mental diffuseness}}; the Tathāgatas are free of proliferation.
**Śag_31**
He for whom there is no fixity and no [conceptual] proliferation, who has gone beyond the bond and the bar—that cravingless sage as he wanders, even the world together with its gods does not know.
**Śag_32**
He whose [discursive] musings are burnt away, inwardly free of all discrimination without remainder—he, having transcended attachment and the perception of form, freed from the {{caturyoga:four yokes|kāma, bhava, dṛṣṭi, avidyā}}, comes to no [further] birth.
**Śag_33**
For one who gives, merit grows; for one who is restrained, enmity is not heaped up; the skilful one abandons evil; and through the exhaustion of the {{kleśa:defilements|afflictions}} one is quenched.
**Śag_34**
The not-doing of any evil, the undertaking of the wholesome, the thorough taming of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
**Śag_35**
Of the mind—hard to hold in check, light, alighting wherever it wishes—the taming is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.
**Śag_36**
Skilled in the sign of the mind, he finds the savour of seclusion; the meditator, prudent and mindful, enjoys the bliss of joy free of [worldly] relish.
**Śag_37**
Living by no craft, light, intent on the [true] self, with senses conquered, wholly liberated in every respect; homeless, without possessiveness, free of longing—he who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, wanders alone: that one is a [true] monk.
**Śag_38**
Him who tames the hard-to-tame mind—far-faring, lone-wandering, bodiless, lying in the cave [of the heart]—him I call a {{brāhmaṇa:true brāhmaṇa|the saint or arhat}}.
**Śag_39.1**
[Ajita's question in the {{Pārāyaṇa:Way to the Far Shore|the closing section of the Sutta Nipāta}}:] By what is this world veiled? By what does it not shine forth? What do you call its besmearing, and what is its great fear?
**Śag_39.2**
By ignorance the world is veiled; through heedlessness it does not shine forth. Idle talk I call its besmearing; suffering is its great fear.
**Śag_39.3**
The streams flow on every side; what is the barrier to the streams? Tell of the restraint of the streams—by what is the stream dammed up?
**Śag_39.4**
Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their barrier; I declare the restraint of the streams—by wisdom indeed is it dammed up.
**Śag_39.5**
Of wisdom and of mindfulness, and of {{nāmarūpa:name-and-form|the psycho-physical complex}} altogether—tell me this, since I ask: where does this cease?
**Śag_39.6**
Wisdom and mindfulness, and name-and-form altogether—through the cessation of consciousness, here it is that this ceases.

title: Śarīrārthagāthā
text:
**Śag_39.7**
For the mindful one as he goes about, how does consciousness cease? Tell me this, since I ask, exactly as it is, beyond doubt.
**Śag_39.8**
For one who does not take delight in feeling, whether inward or outward—thus, for the mindful one as he goes about, consciousness ceases.
**Śag_39.9**
Those who have fully reckoned the dharmas [the adepts beyond training], and those various ones who are still trainees—of their conduct, [tell] me, the prudent one; being asked, declare it, good sir.
**Śag_39.10**
Let him not be greedy amid sensual pleasures; let him be undisturbed in mind; skilful in all dharmas, mindful, let the monk wander forth.
**Śag_40.1**
[A verse from the {{Arthavargīya:Aṭṭhakavagga|the 'Octads' section of the Sutta Nipāta}}, taking up sensual desires:] For one who desires sensual pleasures, if that [desire] of his succeeds, then surely he is glad at heart, the mortal, having gained what he longed for.
**Śag_40.2**
But if, for that being who desires and in whom longing has arisen, those sensual pleasures fail, he is racked with pain as one pierced by a dart.
**Śag_40.3**
He who shuns sensual pleasures as one [shuns treading on] a serpent's head with his foot—he, being mindful, fully passes beyond this clinging that is in the world.
**Śag_40.4**
Fields and dwellings and gold, cattle and horses, jewels and earrings, women and slaves—the man who greedily craves these manifold objects of desire,
**Śag_40.5**
him, as the weak, the onrushing floods overwhelm him as the stronger; thereupon suffering pursues him, as water [pours into] a broken boat.
**Śag_40.6**
But he in whom this [craving] is wholly cut off, struck down like the crown of a [felled] palm tree—his sorrows fall away, like a drop of water from a lotus-leaf.
**Śag_41.1**
[The {{Bhadraikarātrī:Auspicious One|the discourse on the auspicious single [night]; Pali Bhaddekaratta}} verse:] Let one not run back after the past, nor yearn for the future; and whatever present dharmas there are, let one clearly discern them, each in its own place. That which is unassailable and unshakeable—the wise one should foster it.
